steps/1.description: Biallelic EYS variants lead to loss of the EYS protein, an extracellular spacer/structural protein in the photoreceptor outer segment zone. EYS is the human ortholog of Drosophila spacemaker (spam/eyes shut), a protein that maintains the open rhabdom architecture between photoreceptors in insect eyes; in the vertebrate retinas examined to date (zebrafish and primate), EYS localizes near the connecting cilium/transition zone and the photoreceptor ciliary axoneme, where it is believed to help maintain the structural integrity of the ciliary compartment and outer segment. The protein contains at least 21 EGF-like domains and five C-terminal laminin G (LamG) domains. Unlike most RP genes, EYS encodes an extracellular/secreted protein rather than an intracellular component of the phototransduction cascade. Loss of EYS disrupts photoreceptor outer segment morphology, likely through a structural scaffolding role at the ciliary interface.

evidence.snippet: The complete loss of eys (spam) converts an open rhabdom system to a closed one, whereas its targeted expression to photoreceptors of a closed system markedly reorganizes the architecture of the compound eyes to resemble an open system
evidence.explanation: The Drosophila ortholog experiments demonstrate that EYS/spam maintains photoreceptor architectural integrity; loss of EYS collapses the inter-photoreceptor space, directly analogous to outer segment disruption in RP25.

evidence.snippet: Immunostaining indicated that EYS localized near the connecting cilium/transition zone in photoreceptors.
evidence.explanation: Provides the vertebrate localization data behind this node: EYS sits near the connecting cilium/transition zone, the compartment the node is about.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of mutant EYS zebrafish revealed disruption of the ciliary pocket in cone photoreceptors, indicating that EYS is required for maintaining the integrity of the ciliary pocket lumen.
evidence.explanation: Loss of EYS in a vertebrate retina disrupts the ciliary compartment, supporting the structural-disruption claim of this node.

evidence.snippet: EYS was observed at the ciliary axoneme in Y79 ciliated cells
evidence.explanation: Human photoreceptor-like (Y79) cells place the human EYS protein at the ciliary axoneme, the closest human-derived support for the ciliary localization claim.

evidence.snippet: these results point to a novel role for EYS in maintaining the morphological structure of F-actin and in protein transport
evidence.explanation: Supports the protein-transport component of this node (annotated as abnormal protein localization to cilium and intraciliary transport), on zebrafish data.

steps/2.description: EYS localizes near the connecting cilium/transition zone of photoreceptors and to the ciliary axoneme, shown by immunostaining in zebrafish and primate retina and in ciliated human Y79 photoreceptor-like cells. The connecting cilium is the narrow bridge linking the photoreceptor inner segment (biosynthetic compartment) to the outer segment (disc-containing phototransduction compartment); it is functionally equivalent to the transition zone of primary cilia. In zebrafish, loss of EYS disrupts the ciliary pocket of cone photoreceptors and mislocalizes outer segment proteins, indicating a requirement for EYS in maintaining this compartment and in delivering outer segment components; the corresponding localization and transport claims for human photoreceptors are inferred from these non-human vertebrate and cell-line data rather than directly demonstrated. On this basis EYS is treated as a photoreceptor-restricted ciliopathy gene. In Drosophila, the ortholog spam/eyes shut maintains the physical separation between rhabdomeric photoreceptors in the open rhabdom; without it, photoreceptors collapse together.

evidence.snippet: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is an inherited retinal dystrophy leading to progressive loss of the photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium and resulting in blindness usually after several decades.
evidence.explanation: Orphanet establishes progressive photoreceptor loss as the defining pathophysiological feature of retinitis pigmentosa including EYS-RP.

steps/3.description: Structural disruption of the photoreceptor outer segment and connecting cilium resulting from EYS deficiency produces progressive rod photoreceptor death via apoptosis, the final common pathway of rod-cone dystrophies. Rods are the primary affected cell type because EYS is expressed in both rod and cone photoreceptors but the initial rod-predominant degeneration produces the characteristic nyctalopia and peripheral field loss of retinitis pigmentosa. Secondary cone degeneration follows as rods are lost, converting night blindness to broader visual field loss and ultimately severe central visual impairment.

evidence.snippet: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is an inherited retinal dystrophy leading to progressive loss of the photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium and resulting in blindness usually after several decades.
evidence.explanation: Progressive loss of both rod and cone photoreceptors is the established natural history of retinitis pigmentosa; secondary cone degeneration following rod loss explains the progression from nyctalopia to complete blindness.

steps/4.description: Progressive loss of rod photoreceptors leads to non-cell-autonomous secondary cone degeneration. Rods provide trophic support to cones and maintain normal outer retinal oxygen tension; as rods are lost, elevated oxygen levels in the outer retina and loss of rod-derived survival factors drive cone photoreceptor death. This converts the initial rod-dominant disease (nyctalopia, peripheral field loss) to central vision impairment and legal blindness.

evidence.snippet: GRIN1 encodes GluN1, the essential subunit of the N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor.
evidence.explanation: GRIN1 encodes the essential (obligatory) GluN1 subunit of the NMDA receptor, so variants perturb the receptor directly.

evidence.snippet: Mutations cluster within transmembrane segments and result in loss of channel function of varying severity with a dominant-negative effect.
evidence.explanation: De novo GRIN1 missense variants cluster in transmembrane segments and alter channel function.

steps/1.description: De novo heterozygous missense variants (clustered in the transmembrane, pore, and ligand-binding domains) or biallelic missense/truncating variants in GRIN1 alter GluN1, the obligatory subunit of the NMDA receptor. Because every NMDA receptor contains two GluN1 subunits, these variants perturb the glutamate-gated, calcium-permeable channel that mediates excitatory neurotransmission across the developing brain.

evidence.snippet: Three of the mutations increased agonist potency while one reduced proton inhibition of the receptor.
evidence.explanation: Polymicrogyria-associated GRIN1 variants increased agonist potency, a gain-of-function change in receptor activity.

evidence.snippet: All 48 variants in M3 for which comprehensive testing was completed produce a gain-of-function (28/48) compared to loss-of-function (9/48); 11 variants had an indeterminant phenotype.
evidence.explanation: GRIN1/GRIN2 M3-helix variants predominantly enhance channel gating, a gain-of-function mechanism.

steps/2.description: A subset of GRIN1 missense variants increases NMDA receptor activity by enhancing agonist potency, increasing channel open probability and calcium permeability, or reducing voltage-dependent magnesium and proton inhibition, producing excessive NMDA-receptor-mediated current and calcium influx.

evidence.snippet: Our analyses of de novo mutations are consistent with a dominant-negative effect resulting in a significant loss of receptor function.
evidence.explanation: Functional analysis of de novo GRIN1 variants demonstrated loss of receptor function with a dominant-negative effect.

evidence.snippet: As the NMDAR obligatorily contains 2 GluN1 subunits, truncation or lack of both GRIN1 alleles would result in a knock-out and complete deprivation of the NMDAR.
evidence.explanation: Biallelic loss of GluN1 abolishes the obligatory subunit and therefore the NMDA receptor.

steps/3.description: Other GRIN1 variants reduce NMDA receptor function: de novo missense variants lower agonist potency and maximal current (frequently with a dominant-negative effect on hetero-oligomeric receptors), while biallelic truncating variants abolish receptor assembly. Because two GluN1 subunits are obligatory, loss of both alleles produces a functional NMDA-receptor knockout.

evidence.snippet: Seizures occurred in about two-thirds of cases.
evidence.explanation: Epilepsy affects about two-thirds of individuals, reflecting the cortical excitation-inhibition imbalance produced by disrupted NMDAR signaling.

steps/4.description: Whether from excessive or deficient receptor activity, GRIN1 variants disrupt the tightly regulated NMDA-receptor-mediated glutamatergic transmission that developing cortical networks depend on, shifting the balance between excitation and inhibition and producing neuronal hyperexcitability that generates seizures. Seizures occur in roughly two-thirds of individuals with de novo variants.

evidence.snippet: Shared features in the patients were extensive bilateral polymicrogyria associated with severe developmental delay, postnatal microcephaly, cortical visual impairment and intractable epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Gain-of-function GRIN1 variants cause a distinct cortical malformation (extensive bilateral polymicrogyria).

evidence.snippet: Three of the mutations increased agonist potency while one reduced proton inhibition of the receptor.
evidence.explanation: The polymicrogyria-associated variants are gain-of-function with increased agonist potency or reduced proton inhibition.

steps/5.description: A distinct subset of gain-of-function GRIN1 missense variants clustered in the S2 and M3 regions perturbs NMDA-receptor-dependent cortical neurodevelopment, producing a malformation of cortical development (extensive bilateral polymicrogyria); this is the opposite mechanistic direction from the classic loss-of-function route to the disorder.

evidence.snippet: GRIN1-related neurodevelopmental disorder (GRIN1-NDD) is characterized by mild-to-profound developmental delay / intellectual disability (DD/ID) in all affected individuals.
evidence.explanation: Developmental delay / intellectual disability occurs in all affected individuals, the core neurodevelopmental outcome.

evidence.snippet: These 23 individuals presented with a distinct phenotype of profound developmental delay, severe intellectual disability with absent speech, muscular hypotonia, hyperkinetic movement disorder, oculogyric crises, cortical blindness, generalized cerebral atrophy, and epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: The characteristic constellation of severe neurodevelopmental features defines the disorder.

steps/6.description: Dysregulated NMDA-receptor signaling impairs activity-dependent synaptic maturation, plasticity, and cortical development, producing the disorder's core neurodevelopmental phenotype: profound developmental delay / intellectual disability with absent speech, muscular hypotonia, hyperkinetic and stereotypic movement disorders, cortical visual impairment, and, in a subset, a malformation of cortical development (polymicrogyria).

edges/2.description: Other missense variants, and biallelic missense/truncating variants, reduce receptor function.

Heterozygous GRIN1 truncation/haploinsufficiency, in contrast, is tolerated and does not by itself cause the disorder.
