evidence.snippet: Overall, 73% of the malignant peritoneal mesotheliomas analyzed carried at least one inactivated BAP1 allele
evidence.explanation: Large peritoneal mesothelioma series confirms that BAP1 alteration is a dominant recurrent genetic event.

genes/0.notes: BAP1 is the dominant recurrently altered tumor suppressor in peritoneal mesothelioma and may be inactivated by mutation, copy-number loss, or both.

evidence.snippet: Additional recurrently mutated genes in this cohort of malignant peritoneal mesotheliomas included NF2 (3/13), SETD2 (2/13), and DDX3X (2/13).
evidence.explanation: Human tumor profiling identifies SETD2 as a recurrently mutated epigenetic regulator in malignant peritoneal mesothelioma.

genes/1.notes: SETD2 alteration identifies an epigenetic-regulator subset within peritoneal mesothelioma.

evidence.snippet: The molecular profile of MPeM was similar to MPM, with the distinction that PBRM1 alterations occurred at higher frequency (16% v 7%, P < .01).
evidence.explanation: Large-scale molecular profiling identifies PBRM1 alteration as a site-enriched genomic feature of peritoneal mesothelioma.

genes/2.notes: PBRM1 alterations are enriched in peritoneal relative to pleural mesothelioma.

evidence.snippet: ALK rearrangements were only observed in MPeM.
evidence.explanation: Large-scale profiling identifies ALK rearrangement as a site-restricted molecular feature of malignant peritoneal mesothelioma.

genes/3.notes: ALK rearrangements define a rare molecular subtype observed in peritoneal but not pleural mesothelioma in large profiling cohorts.

evidence.snippet: Losses in 3p (BAP1 gene), 9p (CDKN2A) and 22q (NF2) were seen in tumors from both tumor sites, although CDKN2A and NF2 losses were seen at a higher rate in pleural disease (p<0.01).
evidence.explanation: Comparative genomic profiling shows that CDKN2A loss occurs in peritoneal mesothelioma but is relatively less frequent than in pleural disease.

genes/4.notes: CDKN2A loss occurs in peritoneal mesothelioma but is less prevalent than in pleural mesothelioma and is enriched in nonepithelioid disease.

evidence.snippet: Upfront CRS and HIPEC should be considered when achievable, waiting for stronger level of scientific evidence.
evidence.explanation: Multi-institutional retrospective data support upfront cytoreductive surgery as part of curative-intent management when feasible.

treatments/0.description: Upfront maximal cytoreduction is favored when complete or near-complete resection is achievable in carefully selected patients.

evidence.snippet: The panel unanimously recommended CRS-HIPEC for a carefully selected subset of DMPM patients, emphasizing that this approach offers the best potential for improved survival compared to systemic chemotherapy alone.
evidence.explanation: Multisocietal consensus recommends HIPEC as part of the preferred locoregional treatment strategy for selected patients with diffuse malignant peritoneal mesothelioma.

treatments/1.description: HIPEC is paired with cytoreductive surgery in carefully selected resectable diffuse peritoneal mesothelioma and is part of the accepted locoregional standard-of-care strategy.

evidence.snippet: Overall response rate and disease control rate were 45.8% and 91.7%, respectively. Median progression-free survival and median overall survival were 11.0 months and 15.8 months, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Retrospective first-line series demonstrates meaningful disease control with pemetrexed-cisplatin in malignant peritoneal mesothelioma.

treatments/2.description: Platinum-antifolate chemotherapy is an active systemic option for unresectable disease and for patients who are not candidates for curative locoregional treatment.

evidence.snippet: AtezoBev showed promising and durable efficacy in patients with advanced MPeM with an acceptable safety profile.
evidence.explanation: Phase II trial data support atezolizumab-bevacizumab as an active systemic option in previously treated advanced malignant peritoneal mesothelioma.

treatments/3.description: Combined PD-L1 and VEGF blockade has shown activity in advanced unresectable malignant peritoneal mesothelioma after prior platinum-pemetrexed chemotherapy.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of DICER1 is established by identification of a heterozygous germline DICER1 pathogenic variant that is known or suspected to cause loss of function.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews defines the predisposition state modelled by this node as a heterozygous germline loss-of-function DICER1 variant.

evidence.snippet: One hundred and three individuals with a germline P/LP variant developed a primary ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor at a median age of 14 years (range: 11 months-66 years); 13% were diagnosed before 8 years of age, the current age of onset of pelvic surveillance.
evidence.explanation: Registry data quantify SLCT incidence and age distribution among germline DICER1 variant carriers, grounding this node in a human predisposed cohort.

evidence.snippet: Nearly all (36/37) SLCTs and 4/4 GAB tested had a DICER1 mutation in an RNase IIIb domain hotspot; approximately half of these individuals had a predisposing germline DICER1 mutation.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies what fraction of the somatic-hotspot tumors sit on a germline predisposing background - roughly half - which is what makes this node a real but non-obligatory first step rather than a universal one.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous germline loss-of-function DICER1 variant establishes the predisposed state. Penetrance is reduced and age-related, and ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors are among the most characteristic manifestations, with SLCT diagnosed at a median age of 14 years in a large international registry cohort. The germline variant is the first hit; the somatic RNase IIIb hotspot change is the second.

evidence.snippet: DICER1 mutations in the RNase IIIb domain were found in 30 of 102 nonepithelial ovarian tumors (29%), predominantly in Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors (26 of 43, or 60%), including 4 tumors with additional germline DICER1 mutations.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the frequency of the RNase IIIb hotspot lesion in SLCT specifically and its co-occurrence with germline variants.

evidence.snippet: These mutations were restricted to codons encoding metal-binding sites within the RNase IIIb catalytic centers, which are critical for microRNA interaction and cleavage, and were somatic in all 16 samples in which germline DNA was available for testing.
evidence.explanation: Pins the lesion to the metal-binding residues of the RNase IIIb catalytic centre and establishes its somatic origin.

evidence.snippet: The mutant DICER1 proteins had reduced RNase IIIb activity but retained RNase IIIa activity.
evidence.explanation: In vitro cleavage assays support the DECREASED (not abolished) RNase III activity annotated on this node.

steps/2.description: Somatic missense mutations cluster tightly in the DICER1 region encoding the RNase IIIb domain, and are restricted to the codons encoding the four metal-binding residues of the RNase IIIb catalytic centre that are critical for microRNA interaction and cleavage. These mutations were found in 60% of Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors in the founding series and are somatic in every case with germline DNA available. Crucially they do not abolish DICER1: the mutant proteins retain RNase IIIa activity while losing RNase IIIb activity, so this is a hypomorphic, activity-altering lesion rather than a classic null.

evidence.snippet: Further, miRNA profiles showed that mutant DICER1 results in a dramatic loss in processing of mature 5p miRNA strands but were still able to create 3p strand miRNAs.
evidence.explanation: Directly measures the selective loss of 5p-strand processing that defines this node.

evidence.snippet: We further propose that this resulting 3p strand bias in mature miRNA expression likely underpins the oncogenic potential of these hotspot mutations.
evidence.explanation: States the authors' proposed mechanistic link from strand bias to oncogenesis.

steps/3.description: All four metal-binding hotspot alleles are functionally equivalent and behave as hypomorphs: cells expressing them lose mature 5p-strand miRNA production almost completely while still generating 3p-strand miRNAs. The resulting global 3p strand bias in the mature miRNA repertoire, rather than a wholesale loss of miRNA processing, is proposed to underpin the oncogenic effect.

evidence.snippet: Messenger RNA (mRNA) profile changes were consistent with the loss of 5p strand miRNAs and showed enriched expression for predicted targets of the lost 5p-derived miRNAs.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates derepression of the predicted 5p-miRNA targets, which is the content of this node.

evidence.snippet: These mutations do not obliterate DICER1 function but alter it in specific cell types, a novel mechanism through which perturbation of microRNA processing may be oncogenic.
evidence.explanation: Supports the cell-type-selective character of the mechanism, which is why the lesion produces a gonadal stromal tumor rather than a generalized phenotype.

steps/4.description: Loss of the 5p-derived miRNAs releases their target mRNAs from post-transcriptional repression. Messenger RNA profiling of hotspot-mutant cells shows enriched expression of the predicted targets of exactly those lost 5p miRNAs, so the transcriptomic consequence is a specific derepression signature rather than generalized dysregulation. This altered post-transcriptional program in the developing gonadal stroma is the proximate route to tumor formation.

evidence.snippet: DICER1 RNase IIIb domain mutations were identified in 18/41 (44%; 17 moderately, 1 poorly differentiated), including all cases with retiform or heterologous elements.
evidence.explanation: Ties the DICER1 genotype to moderately/poorly differentiated morphology and to all retiform/heterologous tumors.

evidence.snippet: We undertook DICER1 molecular testing in a cohort of 18 well-differentiated SLCTs and show all these to be DICER1 wild-type.
evidence.explanation: Negative result establishing that the DICER1 chain does not extend to well-differentiated SLCT, which is why this entry is scoped to the malignant class.

evidence.snippet: We have confirmed that DICER1 mutations are characteristic of moderately and poorly differentiated SLCTs, while well-differentiated SLCTs may represent a distinct entity.
evidence.explanation: Independent 37-case replication of the grade restriction of the DICER1 driver, the observation this entry's malignant-class scoping rests on.

steps/5.description: The DICER1-mutant tumors are moderately or poorly differentiated, and every tumor with retiform or heterologous elements in a 42-case molecular series carried a DICER1 RNase IIIb mutation. The genotype therefore tracks with exactly the morphologic features that carry malignant potential, and well-differentiated SLCT — which is DICER1 wild-type — falls outside this chain.

evidence.snippet: This type of tumor predominates in the 2nd and 3rd decades of life and usually presents with hormonal changes, including signs of virilization, such as amenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, and male pattern of pilification.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the virilizing manifestations that this node produces, and the age distribution of the tumor.

evidence.snippet: These characteristics are due to an increase in androgen production by tumor cells.
evidence.explanation: States the causal attribution of the virilizing phenotype to tumor androgen output, which is the mechanistic content of this node.

evidence.snippet: DICER1-mutant patients trended toward having more androgenic symptoms (P=0.22).
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL: a non-significant trend (P=0.22), quoted with its p-value so the weakness is visible. It is suggestive, not established, that the DICER1 genotype preferentially produces the androgenic presentation.

steps/6.description: Functional SLCTs secrete androgen from their Leydig-cell-like component, raising circulating testosterone and producing hirsutism, androgenic alopecia, and amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea. Some patients instead show hyperestrogenism, either from direct tumor estrogen secretion or from peripheral aromatization of tumor-derived testosterone. DICER1-mutant tumors trended toward more androgenic symptoms than their FOXL2-mutant counterparts.

edges/2.description: In a predisposed gonad the second, somatic hotspot hit in the retained allele completes the two-step genetic lesion.

edges/3.description: RNase IIIb is the domain that cleaves the 3' end of the 5p miRNA strand, so its selective inactivation removes mature 5p miRNAs while leaving 3p production intact.

edges/4.description: Transcripts normally repressed by the lost 5p-derived miRNAs become enriched in expression.

edges/5.description: The derepressed program drives outgrowth of a tumor recapitulating testicular tubular and interstitial differentiation.

edges/6.description: The Leydig-like interstitial component of the tumor secretes androgen, producing the virilizing clinical picture.

evidence.snippet: Somatic missense mutations affecting the RNase IIIb domain of DICER1 are common in nonepithelial ovarian tumors.
evidence.explanation: States the core gene-disease association curated here.

evidence.snippet: DICER1 and FOXL2 mutations were mutually exclusive.
evidence.explanation: Establishes mutual exclusivity of the two sex cord-stromal drivers within SLCT, the observation that underpins keeping the driver-defined histotypes as separate Disease entries.

evidence.snippet: The molecular analysis showed DICER1 mutations in 54.5% of cases, and a FOXL2 mutation in 6% of tumors. In addition, we detected 2 cases with TERT promoter mutation.
evidence.explanation: Reports TERT promoter mutation alongside the DICER1 and FOXL2 frequencies in the same 37-tumor cohort.

evidence.snippet: Most of the ovarian SLCTs are unilateral, and their treatment is preferably surgical.
evidence.explanation: Supports surgery as the primary treatment modality.

treatments/0.description: Because SLCTs are unilateral, stage I, and occur in young women, unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the procedure of choice when fertility preservation is desired, and surgery alone is usually curative.

evidence.snippet: Unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the procedure of choice for patients that want to preserve their fertility.
evidence.explanation: States the recommended fertility-sparing surgical procedure for this tumor.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Excision of the affected ovary removes the tumor, which is the definitive treatment for stage I disease.

evidence.snippet: A total of 2 (16.7%) patients received adjuvant treatment; 1 of them underwent 3 cycles of paclitaxel and carboplatin every 21 days, and the other underwent 4 cycles of ifosfamide, cisplatin and etoposide every 21 days.
evidence.explanation: Documents the selective use of adjuvant chemotherapy and the specific regimens given in a consecutive series.

evidence.snippet: Ovarian tumors require surgery and may also require chemotherapy depending on stage and histology, with radiation generally reserved for relapsed disease.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management guidance confirming stage- and histology-dependent use of chemotherapy in DICER1-related ovarian tumors.

treatments/1.description: Chemotherapy is added selectively for higher-stage or poorly differentiated tumors rather than routinely. Regimens used in reported series include carboplatin-paclitaxel and ifosfamide-cisplatin-etoposide.

evidence.snippet: DICER1-related ovarian tumors were detected before 8 years of age, prompting the Registry to recommend earlier initiation of ovarian surveillance with pelvic ultrasound beginning at the time of detection of a germline DICER1 P/LP variant.
evidence.explanation: States the current surveillance recommendation and the registry finding that motivated it.

evidence.snippet: Pelvic ultrasounds for gynecologic tumors in females every six months until at least age 40 years.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews surveillance schedule for gynecologic tumors in DICER1 variant carriers.

treatments/2.description: Carriers of a germline DICER1 pathogenic variant undergo periodic pelvic ultrasound to detect ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors early. Registry data showing that 13% of SLCTs were diagnosed before age 8 — the previous surveillance start age — prompted a recommendation to begin ovarian surveillance at the time the germline variant is identified.

evidence.snippet: Once a germline DICER1 pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, predictive testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: Supports cascade genetic testing of relatives once a germline variant is found.

evidence.snippet: Three children of women with SLCT were diagnosed with PPB based on genetic testing and clinical screening during the course of this study. All were diagnosed with PPB in its earliest and most curable form (Type I), were treated with surgery alone, and are alive without evidence of disease.
evidence.explanation: Documents the concrete yield of cascade testing triggered by an SLCT diagnosis: three children detected with pleuropulmonary blastoma at its most curable stage. This is the strongest available justification for testing after SLCT.

treatments/3.description: A diagnosis of moderately or poorly differentiated SLCT is an indication to consider germline DICER1 testing, since the tumor is a sentinel neoplasm of an autosomal dominant predisposition syndrome with implications for the patient and first-degree relatives.

evidence.snippet: Our data suggest at least 3 molecular subtypes of SLCT with distinct clinicopathologic features: DICER1 mutant (younger, more androgenic symptoms, moderately/poorly differentiated, retiform or heterologous elements), FOXL2 mutant (postmenopausal, abnormal bleeding, moderately/poorly differentiated, no retiform or heterologous elements), and DICER1/FOXL2 wild type (intermediate age, no retiform or heterologous elements, including all well-differentiated tumors).
evidence.explanation: Sets out the three molecular subtypes and the fact that one of them has no identified driver, which is the substance of this knowledge gap.

evidence.snippet: The DICER1WT tumors showed increased expression of PRKCA, HNF1A, LDLR, and MAP2K5. On the contrary, the DICER1MUT cases showed increased expression of CDK6, NOTCH2, and FGFR2.
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL, and a partial narrowing rather than a resolution of this gap: RNA sequencing shows the DICER1-wild-type tumors have a distinct expression program rather than being a residual category, but differential expression identifies candidate genes, not a driver lesion, so the wild-type arm still has no established mechanism.

open_questions/0.rationale: Molecular classification of SLCT identifies at least three groups with distinct clinicopathologic profiles: DICER1-mutant (young, androgenic, retiform or heterologous elements), FOXL2 C134W-mutant (postmenopausal, abnormal bleeding), and double wild-type at intermediate age, which accounts for about 37% of tumors and includes all well-differentiated cases. Only the DICER1 arm has a worked-out mechanism; no driver at all is known for the wild-type group, which is the largest single category after DICER1. This matters for entry granularity as well as biology: if the FOXL2-mutant SLCTs turn out to share the AGCT mechanism, the boundary between this entry and Adult Granulosa Cell Tumor of Ovary is drawn in the wrong place, and the mutual exclusivity of the two drivers within a single morphologic category is currently the main evidence that it is not.

evidence.snippet: In six of eight MCV-positive MCCs, viral DNA was integrated within the tumor genome in a clonal pattern, suggesting that MCV infection and integration preceded clonal expansion of the tumor cells.
evidence.explanation: Establishes clonal integration of MCPyV preceding tumor expansion, the basis of viral T-antigen-driven oncogenesis.

evidence.snippet: tumor-derived virus mutations do not affect retinoblastoma tumor suppressor protein (Rb) binding by LT but do eliminate viral DNA replication capacity.
evidence.explanation: Shows the tumor-specific truncated large T antigen retains RB binding while losing replication capacity, driving proliferation.

steps/0.description: In MCPyV-positive MCC, clonally integrated virus expresses truncated large T antigen (LT) that binds and inactivates RB tumor suppressor protein, releasing E2F transcription factors and driving cell cycle progression. Small T antigen (sT) promotes proliferation through multiple mechanisms including 4E-BP1 hyperphosphorylation and cap-dependent translation.

evidence.snippet: MCPyV-negative tumors also displayed high overall mutation burden (10.09 ± 2.32 mutations/Mb) and were characterized by a prominent UV-signature pattern with C > T transitions comprising 85% of mutations.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the high UV-signature mutational burden that drives virus-negative MCC.

steps/1.description: In virus-negative MCC (approximately 20%), high levels of UV-induced mutations (C>T transitions at dipyrimidine sites) drive oncogenesis. These tumors have among the highest tumor mutational burdens of any cancer and frequently harbor mutations in TP53, RB1, and other tumor suppressors.

evidence.snippet: Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV) may contribute to tumorigenesis in a subset of tumors via inhibition of tumor suppressors such as retinoblastoma (RB1) by mutated viral T antigens
evidence.explanation: Documents RB1 inactivation by viral T antigens as a shared oncogenic route, complemented by somatic RB1 mutation in virus-negative MCC.

steps/2.description: In virus-positive MCC, viral large T antigen binds and inactivates RB1 protein. In virus-negative MCC, RB1 is frequently inactivated by somatic mutations. In both cases, loss of RB1 function releases E2F transcription factors to drive cell cycle progression and proliferation.

steps/3.description: Whether driven by viral T antigens or UV-induced mutations, MCC cells exhibit uncontrolled proliferation. The neuroendocrine differentiation is retained, with expression of characteristic markers including CK20, chromogranin, and synaptophysin.

edges/0.description: Viral LT antigen sequesters and inactivates pRB protein

edges/1.description: E2F activation drives expression of cell cycle genes

evidence.snippet: Nine MCC tumor-derived LT genomic sequences have been examined, and all were found to harbor mutations prematurely truncating the MCV LT helicase.
evidence.explanation: Tumor-specific truncating LT mutations define the MCPyV T-antigen driver signature in MCC.

genes/0.notes: In MCPyV-positive MCC, viral small T and truncated large T antigens are the primary oncogenic drivers. Large T antigen binds RB1, while small T antigen promotes proliferation through multiple mechanisms. Tumors are addicted to viral oncoprotein expression.

evidence.snippet: In addition to previously identified mutations in TP53, RB1, and PIK3CA, we discovered activating mutations of oncogenes, including HRAS and loss-of-function mutations in PRUNE2 and NOTCH family genes in MCPyV-negative MCC.
evidence.explanation: Confirms recurrent somatic RB1 (and TP53) mutations in virus-negative MCC.

genes/1.notes: RB1 mutations occur in the majority of MCPyV-negative MCC but are virtually absent in virus-positive tumors, where viral LT antigen functionally inactivates RB1 protein.

evidence.snippet: In addition to previously identified mutations in TP53, RB1, and PIK3CA, we discovered activating mutations of oncogenes, including HRAS and loss-of-function mutations in PRUNE2 and NOTCH family genes in MCPyV-negative MCC.
evidence.explanation: Confirms recurrent somatic TP53 mutations in virus-negative MCC, alongside the UV mutational signature.

genes/2.notes: TP53 mutations with UV signature are common in virus-negative MCC. Virus-positive tumors retain wild-type TP53, suggesting different selective pressures.

evidence.snippet: Avelumab | Accepted_Therapeutic_Use_For | - | - | locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma; metastatic Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC); advanced renal cell carcinoma (RCC).
evidence.explanation: NCI Thesaurus asserts accepted therapeutic use of avelumab for metastatic Merkel cell carcinoma.

treatments/0.description: Anti-PD-L1 antibody approved for metastatic MCC. First immune checkpoint inhibitor approved for MCC based on durable responses in the JAVELIN Merkel 200 trial. Response rates of approximately 30-35% in previously treated patients and higher in first-line setting.

evidence.snippet: The response rate was 62% among patients with MCPyV-positive tumors (10 of 16 patients) and 44% among those with virus-negative tumors (4 of 9 patients).
evidence.explanation: First-line pembrolizumab produced durable responses in both virus-positive and virus-negative advanced MCC.

treatments/1.description: Anti-PD-1 antibody approved for advanced MCC. Response rates of approximately 50-70% with durable responses. Both virus-positive and virus-negative MCC respond to checkpoint inhibition.

treatments/2.description: Wide local excision with adequate margins (1-2 cm) is the primary treatment for localized MCC. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is recommended given high rate of occult nodal metastases.

treatments/3.description: MCC is radiosensitive. Adjuvant radiation improves local control, particularly for tumors with high-risk features. Radiation may be used as primary treatment for unresectable tumors.

treatments/4.description: MCC is chemosensitive (like other small cell carcinomas) with initial response rates of 50-60% to platinum/etoposide regimens. However, responses are typically short-lived and chemotherapy has been largely supplanted by immunotherapy.

evidence.snippet: We report a patient who presented with clinical and biochemical phenotypic features that overlap cblX, but who does not have any mutations in either MMACHC or HCFC1.
evidence.explanation: How the gene was reached, and why the case is a cblX phenocopy rather than a cblX case: the two genes that were already known to cause this picture were excluded first.

steps/1.description:
A homozygous missense change in the THAP domain, the zinc-finger DNA-binding module shared across the twelve human THAP proteins. The variant was found after MMACHC and HCFC1 had been sequenced and excluded in a patient whose clinical and biochemical picture overlapped cblX, so the gene was reached by elimination plus a mechanistic hypothesis rather than by an unbiased screen.
p.Phe80Leu is the only reported MAHCL allele. No second family, no null allele, and no allelic series exist, so nothing is known about whether other THAP11 variants would give the same disease.

evidence.snippet: We show that THAP11F80L selectively affected promoter binding by THAP11, having more deleterious effects on a subset of THAP11 targets, and resulting in altered patterns of gene expression.
evidence.explanation: The selectivity of the binding defect, which is what allows a general transcription factor variant to produce a pathway-specific disease.

steps/2.description: The step that turns a transcription factor variant into a metabolic disease, and the one place in this entry where the causal claim is directly measured rather than inferred. In HEK-293 cells the F80L protein bound a subset of THAP11 target promoters less well than wild type, and the MMACHC promoter was among the strongly affected ones. Binding was selectively rather than globally impaired, which matters: a transcription factor that had simply stopped working everywhere would not explain a disease whose dominant biochemical signature is a single pathway.

evidence.snippet: HCFC1 regulates cobalamin metabolism via the regulation of MMACHC expression through its interaction with THAP11, a THAP domain-containing transcription factor.
evidence.explanation: The regulatory axis itself, stated in the report that identified the THAP11 patient.

evidence.snippet: The severe reduction in MMACHC mRNA and protein within subject fibroblast lines suggested a role for HCFC1 in transcriptional regulation of MMACHC, which was further supported by the identification of consensus HCFC1 binding sites in MMACHC.
evidence.explanation: The measurement of reduced MMACHC message and protein in patient fibroblasts. Graded as evidence for the pathway rather than for MAHCL: these are cblX patients with HCFC1 variants, not the THAP11 patient, so it establishes what the complex does and not what this disease does.

evidence.snippet: Since HCFC1/RONIN jointly regulate MMACHC, patients with mutations in these factors suffer from reduced MMACHC expression and exhibit a cblC-like disease.
evidence.explanation: States the joint regulation and the phenocopy relationship that the whole entry turns on. RONIN is the alternative name for THAP11.

steps/3.description: MMACHC transcription falls even though the MMACHC gene is intact. This is the same lesion cblX produces through HCFC1, and the two were shown to converge here: HCFC1 and THAP11 act as a complex on the MMACHC promoter, and knocking down either one reduces MMACHC message.

evidence.snippet: Cobalamin disorder is an inborn vitamin deficiency characterized by neurodevelopmental abnormalities, most often owing to biallelic mutations in the MMACHC gene, whose gene product MMACHC is a key enzyme in the cobalamin (vitamin B12) metabolic pathway.
evidence.explanation: MMACHC's position in the pathway, which is what makes reduced MMACHC expression a metabolic lesion rather than merely a transcriptional observation.

evidence.snippet: MMACHC, a cytosolic cobalamin trafficking chaperone, has been shown recently to catalyze a reductive decyanation reaction when it encounters cyanocobalamin.
evidence.explanation: The decyanation half of the chemistry this node describes, which the previous citation did not support: the earlier item establishes only that MMACHC is a key enzyme in the pathway.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrate that this versatile protein catalyzes an entirely different chemical reaction with alkylcobalamins using the thiolate of glutathione for nucleophilic displacement to generate cob(I)alamin and the corresponding glutathione thioether
evidence.explanation: The glutathione-dependent dealkylation half, and the product cob(I)alamin that the downstream cofactor synthesis depends on.

steps/4.description:
MMACHC is the cytosolic chaperone that processes incoming cobalamin, removing the upper axial ligand from cyanocobalamin, methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin so the cofactor can be routed onward. Without enough of it, dietary and therapeutic cobalamin cannot be converted into the two active forms the cell needs.
This node and everything below it are inherited from cblC biology rather than measured in a MAHCL patient. That is a legitimate inference, because the complementation behaviour and biochemistry of the transcriptional disorders match cblC, but it is an inference and the entry does not present it otherwise.

evidence.snippet: Functional analysis in the developing zebrafish embryo demonstrated that both THAP11 and HCFC1 regulate the proliferation and differentiation of neural precursors, suggesting important roles in normal brain development.
evidence.explanation: The neural developmental role, measured in zebrafish.

evidence.snippet: In addition to exhibiting loss of Mmachc, metabolic perturbations, and developmental defects previously observed in cblC, we uncovered reduced expression of target genes that encode ribosome protein subunits.
evidence.explanation: The second arm of the same transcriptional lesion, found in mouse models of both genes. Described as non-MMACHC rather than non-metabolic, since no rescue by MMACHC has been reported for the ribosomal phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: the hcfc1b-mediated craniofacial abnormalities were rescued by expression of human MMACHC, a downstream target of HCFC1 that is aberrantly expressed in cblX
evidence.explanation: Graded REFUTE against the strong reading of this node, that the developmental branch is independent of the cobalamin lesion. It is not: the craniofacial phenotype in the companion zebrafish model is rescued by MMACHC, so it runs at least partly through the same downstream gene. The node's description was corrected rather than the evidence omitted.

steps/5.description:
A parallel branch, and the reason MAHCL may not be simply a metabolic disease with a neurological complication. THAP11 loss in zebrafish impairs proliferation and differentiation of neural precursors, and separately abolishes Meckel's cartilage and the pharyngeal cartilages. Mouse work on Hcfc1 and Ronin found the same complex regulating ribosome protein genes, with phenotypes attributed to deregulated ribosome biogenesis rather than to the metabolic block.
How independent this branch really is from the metabolic one is not settled, and the honest answer is less independent than it first looks. In the companion zebrafish work on hcfc1b, the craniofacial abnormalities were rescued by expressing human MMACHC, and the authors concluded that the craniofacial role is mediated in part through MMACHC regulation. So at least some of what looks like a separate developmental program runs back through the same downstream gene as the metabolic lesion. The ribosome biogenesis arm has no such rescue reported and remains the clearest candidate for a genuinely MMACHC-independent contribution.
Whether this branch contributes to the human phenotype is unknown, because there is one patient and no craniofacial or ribosomal assessment was reported for them.

evidence.snippet: Defects in cobalamin metabolism lead to disorders characterized by the accumulation of methylmalonic acid and/or homocysteine in blood and urine.
evidence.explanation: The shared biochemical consequence of the cobalamin disorders. Note the "and/or", which is the literature's own acknowledgement that the pairing is not obligate, and which bears on the knowledge gap about this disease's name.

steps/6.description: Because MMACHC sits upstream of the branch point, losing it starves both downstream enzymes at once: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase loses adenosylcobalamin and methionine synthase loses methylcobalamin. That dual failure is what makes the cblC-type disorders "combined", and it is why the biochemical signature is methylmalonic acid plus homocysteine rather than either alone.

steps/7.description:
Mild methylmalonic aciduria was recorded in the single reported patient. It is milder than in classical cblC, and the OMIM clinical synopsis for this disorder notes it occurred without homocystinuria, which is unusual for a disorder in this group.
The source is the OMIM clinical synopsis recorded in external_assertions, not a quotable sentence: the primary report's cached record is abstract-only and its abstract does not give the patient's biochemistry. This phenotype therefore carries no evidence item rather than one that would attest to something else. The GeneReviews sentence naming methylmalonic acid and total homocysteine as the mainstays of biochemical testing is a testing strategy rather than an observation about this patient, and lives in the diagnosis block.

evidence.snippet: A common phenotype of severe neurological symptoms including intractable epilepsy and profound neurocognitive impairment, along with variable biochemical manifestations, was observed in all affected subjects compared to individuals with early-onset cblC.
evidence.explanation: The neurological severity of the transcriptional cobalamin disorders, measured in the cblX cohort. Cited for the comparison class rather than for this disease, because the MAHCL patient's phenotype is only described as overlapping cblX.

steps/8.description: Profoundly impaired neurodevelopment with seizures. The phenotype was described as overlapping cblX, and cblX itself is characterised by intractable epilepsy and profound neurocognitive impairment that is more severe than in early-onset cblC. Whether MAHCL tracks cblX or cblC in severity is not established from one patient.

evidence.snippet: In particular, THAP11F80L exhibited a strong effect on association with the MMACHC promoter and led to a decrease in MMACHC gene transcription, suggesting that the THAP11F80L mutation is directly responsible for the observed cobalamin disorder.
evidence.explanation: Evidence for this specific edge rather than for either node: the same experiment measures reduced promoter association and the resulting fall in transcription, and the authors draw the causal link explicitly.

edges/7.description: Plausible on the model data and unmeasured in the single patient. The alternative, that the developmental impairment is entirely secondary to the cobalamin block, is equally unmeasured.

evidence.snippet: We sequenced THAP11 by Sanger sequencing and discovered a potentially pathogenic, homozygous variant, c.240C > G (p.Phe80Leu).
evidence.explanation: The allele and the reporting authors' own hedged classification of it, which is the basis for LIKELY_PATHOGENIC rather than PATHOGENIC above.

evidence.snippet: THAP11(cblX-like), ZNF143(cblX-like), or a hemizygous variant in HCFC1 (cblX, which can show a cblC complementation class).
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists THAP11 among the genes in which biallelic pathogenic variants confirm a diagnosis of a disorder of intracellular cobalamin metabolism, under the older "cblX-like" designation that predates the cblL name.

genes/0.notes:
The causal gene, also known as RONIN. It encodes a THAP-domain zinc-finger transcription factor that partners with HCFC1. Note the HGNC identifier: THAP11 is hgnc:23194. hgnc:20856 is THAP1, a different THAP-family gene that causes DYT6 dystonia and has nothing to do with cobalamin metabolism. The deep-research report for this entry offered HGNC:20856 as THAP11 in four places, so the trap is worth recording; a separate report in this repository uses the same identifier correctly for THAP1.
That particular form of the error is caught. HGNC is configured in conf/oak_config.yaml, and validate-terms compares a bound label against the ontology's canonical label, so copying the report's identifier together with its offered label fails with a label mismatch. What is not caught is the self-consistent version: hgnc:20856 carrying its own true label THAP1, under a name and preferred_term of THAP11. Nothing compares the gene the binding resolves to against the gene the entry says it is about, so that combination passes schema validation and term validation alike.

evidence.snippet: Recently, mutations in the transcriptional regulators HCFC1 and RONIN (THAP11) were shown to result in cellular phenocopies of cblC.
evidence.explanation: Why MMACHC belongs in this entry at all: the disease is a phenocopy of MMACHC deficiency produced without an MMACHC variant. relationship_type is UNKNOWN rather than CAUSATIVE because the schema has no value for "target of the causal lesion, not itself mutated".

genes/1.notes: Not mutated in this disease. It is listed here because it is the gene whose expression the lesion reduces, and because a reader who sees cblC biochemistry with a normal MMACHC sequence needs the entry to say why.

evidence.snippet: We used exome sequencing to identify the genetic basis of an X-linked form of combined methylmalonic acidemia and hyperhomocysteinemia, designated cblX.
evidence.explanation: Establishes cblX as a separate X-linked entity, which is the distinction this entry has to hold against.

genes/2.notes: The partner gene. Hemizygous HCFC1 variants cause cblX, the X-linked disorder that MAHCL phenocopies through the same complex. Recorded here as a differential rather than as a MAHCL gene.

evidence.snippet: THAP11(cblX-like), ZNF143(cblX-like), or a hemizygous variant in HCFC1 (cblX, which can show a cblC complementation class).
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews listing ZNF143 beside THAP11 in the confirmatory gene list, which is what makes it the nearest differential.

genes/3.notes: The third member of the regulatory complex and the other gene GeneReviews lists as cblX-like. Recorded here as a differential rather than as a MAHCL gene: a patient with cblC biochemistry and a normal MMACHC sequence has THAP11, ZNF143 and HCFC1 to work through, and this entry covers only the first.

evidence.snippet: Critically ill individuals must be stabilized, preferably in consultation with a metabolic specialist, by treating acidosis, reversing catabolism, and initiating parenteral hydroxocobalamin.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews acute management recommendation for this disease group. Cited as group management, not as evidence of benefit in MAHCL, for which none exists.

treatments/0.description: The mainstay of treatment across the disorders of intracellular cobalamin metabolism, given parenterally. No treatment response has been reported for a MAHCL patient, so this is the management of the group the disease belongs to rather than an established therapy for it. Whether raising cobalamin availability helps when the lesion is a shortage of the chaperone that processes it is a real mechanistic question, not a formality.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Increasing substrate availability to a reduced pool of MMACHC chaperone. It does not act on the transcriptional lesion, and nothing reported for MAHCL does.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of thromboembolic complications (e.g., HUS and thrombotic microangiopathy) includes initiation of hydroxocobalamin (OHCbl) and betaine or an increase in their doses.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews naming betaine in the management of this disease group.

evidence.snippet: Hydroxocobalamin (OHCbl), betaine, folinic acid, levocarnitine and eventually dietary protein restriction are the main therapeutic approaches.
evidence.explanation: The standard regimen for the cblC group, of which this is one component. Cited as group management; the study itself is a cblC series, not a MAHCL one.

treatments/1.description:
Betaine provides an alternative route for remethylating homocysteine to methionine through betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase, bypassing the methylcobalamin-dependent methionine synthase reaction that the cobalamin block disables. GeneReviews names it alongside hydroxocobalamin in the management of thromboembolic complications.
As with everything in this section, no treatment response has been reported for a MAHCL patient. Note also that its rationale is aimed at the homocysteine arm, which the single reported patient's OMIM synopsis says was not raised, so it is the part of the group regimen whose applicability to this disorder is least clear.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Bypasses the methylcobalamin-dependent arm of the block by remethylating homocysteine through a cobalamin-independent enzyme. It does nothing for the adenosylcobalamin arm.

evidence.snippet: Hydroxocobalamin (OHCbl), betaine, folinic acid, levocarnitine and eventually dietary protein restriction are the main therapeutic approaches.
evidence.explanation: The regimen this component belongs to, from a cblC treatment series.

treatments/2.description: Part of the standard regimen for the cblC group. No treatment response has been reported for a MAHCL patient.

evidence.snippet: Hydroxocobalamin (OHCbl), betaine, folinic acid, levocarnitine and eventually dietary protein restriction are the main therapeutic approaches.
evidence.explanation: The regimen this component belongs to, from a cblC treatment series.

treatments/3.description: Part of the standard regimen for the cblC group, given to support conjugation and excretion of accumulating acyl species. No treatment response has been reported for a MAHCL patient.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Prolonged fasting (longer than overnight without dextrose-containing intravenous fluids); dietary protein intake below the recommended dietary allowance for age or more than that prescribed by a metabolic specialist; methionine restriction including use of medical foods that do not contain methionine; and the anesthetic nitrous oxide.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews agents-and-circumstances-to-avoid list in full. Quoted rather than summarised because each item is separately actionable and the nitrous oxide entry in particular is a peri-operative safety point.

evidence.snippet: Hydroxocobalamin (OHCbl), betaine, folinic acid, levocarnitine and eventually dietary protein restriction are the main therapeutic approaches.
evidence.explanation: Dietary protein restriction as part of the group regimen.

treatments/4.description:
Dietary protein restriction is part of the group regimen, but the more clinically load-bearing half of this entry is what to avoid, because two of the items are things a clinician unaware of the diagnosis would do routinely.
GeneReviews lists prolonged fasting beyond overnight without dextrose-containing intravenous fluids, protein intake below the age-appropriate allowance or above what a metabolic specialist has prescribed, methionine restriction including medical foods that contain no methionine, and the anaesthetic nitrous oxide. Nitrous oxide is the sharpest of these: it irreversibly oxidises the cobalt of cobalamin and inactivates methionine synthase, so in a patient whose cobalamin processing is already limited it can precipitate acute decompensation. Methionine restriction is the counterintuitive one, since restricting the amino acid a patient is already short of is exactly the wrong move here.
Note the direction of inference. This is management for disorders of intracellular cobalamin metabolism as a class, which MAHCL belongs to by biochemistry; nothing has been reported for a MAHCL patient specifically.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Limits the propiogenic substrate load reaching the blocked methylmalonyl-CoA mutase step, and avoids the exposures that would deepen the functional cobalamin deficit.

evidence.snippet: Defects in cobalamin metabolism lead to disorders characterized by the accumulation of methylmalonic acid and/or homocysteine in blood and urine.
evidence.explanation: The literature's own "and/or", which shows the pairing is not treated as obligate even within the group this disorder is named after.

evidence.snippet: A common phenotype of severe neurological symptoms including intractable epilepsy and profound neurocognitive impairment, along with variable biochemical manifestations, was observed in all affected subjects compared to individuals with early-onset cblC.
evidence.explanation: Biochemical variability was already reported as a feature of the transcriptional cobalamin disorders in the cblX cohort, which makes the MAHCL observation less of an outlier than it looks.

open_questions/0.rationale:
This matters because the biochemical pairing is what places a patient in this disease group in the first place. A newborn screen or a metabolic workup that finds isolated methylmalonic aciduria will not generate a differential that includes the cobalamin complementation groups, and the one MAHCL patient described so far would have looked like that.
Three readings are open and one patient cannot separate them. The mechanism might be quantitative: partial, selective loss of MMACHC transcription could reduce adenosylcobalamin enough to raise methylmalonic acid while leaving methylcobalamin adequate for methionine synthase, which would predict an isolated or methylmalonic-predominant picture as characteristic of the transcriptional disorders rather than as an exception. It might be developmental, with the biochemistry sampled at an age or a treatment state that masked the homocysteine rise. Or the single patient might simply be atypical.
The literature is already hedged here in a way worth noticing: the standard description of the cobalamin disorders speaks of methylmalonic acid "and/or" homocysteine. Naming this entity for both, in the same act as recording a patient who had one, is a nosological decision made by OMIM rather than a finding.
A second reported patient with a full biochemical profile would settle it. There is currently nothing else that would.

evidence.snippet: THAP11(cblX-like), ZNF143(cblX-like), or a hemizygous variant in HCFC1 (cblX, which can show a cblC complementation class).
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews' own framing, which places THAP11 in the biallelic list while still naming it after cblX. Both halves of the tension in one line.

evidence.snippet: We used exome sequencing to identify the genetic basis of an X-linked form of combined methylmalonic acidemia and hyperhomocysteinemia, designated cblX.
evidence.explanation: The X-linked inheritance of cblX, which is the axis of separation.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The two are separated by inheritance and gene and joined by mechanism, and the literature has not settled which of those should decide. GeneReviews still calls THAP11 "cblX-like" rather than giving it its own complementation letter, and clinical gene panels list THAP11 and ZNF143 together under that label; OMIM has since given it a separate number and the cblL name.
This entry follows OMIM and curates cblL separately, for two reasons that are about the knowledge base rather than about nosology. First, inheritance differs, and an entry that merged an X-linked hemizygous disorder with an autosomal recessive one could not carry a coherent inheritance block or support correct recurrence-risk counselling. Second, the surrounding entries already work this way: cblC, cblD, cblE and cblG each have their own entry rather than being subtypes of a cobalamin grouping.
One consequence should be flagged for a curator rather than silently absorbed. `kb/disorders/Inborn_Disorder_of_Cobalamin_Metabolism_and_Transport.yaml` describes THAP11 inside its cblX subtype as a "cblX-like form", which was accurate when written and is now superseded by this entry. Reconciling that description is a separate edit to a shared file and is deliberately not bundled into this PR.

evidence.snippet: HEK-293 cells bearing a THAP11 mutation identified in a patient suffering from cobalamin disorder (THAP11F80L) were viable although proliferated more slowly.
evidence.explanation: The functional work that does exist, done on the patient's own allele, which is the part of this entry that is not inherited from the pathway.

open_questions/2.rationale:
Worth stating explicitly because the entry looks better evidenced than the disease is. The molecular mechanism is genuinely well supported: promoter binding and transcription were measured directly for the patient's own allele in HEK-293 cells, and the regulatory relationship is confirmed in mouse and zebrafish. That is more functional evidence than many single-patient disorders have.
What is missing is everything patient-facing. There is no second family, so penetrance, expressivity and allelic spectrum are unknown and no genotype-phenotype statement is possible. There is no reported treatment response, so the hydroxocobalamin entry in this file is group management applied by inference. And there is a specific mechanistic reason not to assume it transfers: in enzymatic cblC the chaperone is present but defective, whereas here it is scarce but normal, and it is not obvious that saturating a reduced pool of functional chaperone behaves like saturating a normal pool of defective one.
The single most useful thing anyone could add to this entry is a second reported patient.

evidence.snippet: This resulted in the identification of a missense mutation in a conserved residue of the C6ORF66 gene, which encodes a 20.2 kDa mitochondrial protein.
evidence.explanation: The founding allele and the size of the protein it damages.

evidence.snippet: Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous nonsense mutation in NDUFAF4 (c.478G > T; p.Glu160Ter), encoding a mitochondrial complex I assembly factor.
evidence.explanation: The one clearly truncating allele in the series.

steps/1.description: Two damaged copies of NDUFAF4, which encodes a 20.2 kDa mitochondrial protein. The reported alleles span the mutation classes and the length of the protein: the founding c.194T>C p.(Leu65Pro) missense change, a c.7G>C p.(Ala3Pro) change at the extreme N-terminus in the Leigh-syndrome patient, a c.478G>T p.(Glu160Ter) nonsense allele in the siblings with fatal neonatal encephalopathy, and a frameshift c.224del p.(P75Lfs*7) together with a c.413T>C p.(I138T) missense allele in the optic-atrophy families.

evidence.snippet: NDUFAF4 (C6ORF66) is an assembly factor of complex I that associates with assembly intermediates of the Q-module.
evidence.explanation: Where the protein normally sits, which is what this node is about. The sentence is the citing paper's introduction restating a fact established by earlier complexome profiling of human cell lines, so evidence_source grades that underlying in vitro work and quote_role records that this paper is not where it came from.

evidence.snippet: NDUFAF3 and NDUFAF4 are necessary for the early connection of the Q module to ND1
evidence.explanation: The pairing with NDUFAF3 and the specific connection step. The quoted claim comes from complexome profiling studies, which is what evidence_source grades; quote_role records that the 2026 series is synthesising work it did not perform.

steps/2.description: NDUFAF4's normal place in complex I biogenesis is on the Q-module intermediates, where it associates early and stays until just before the enzyme is completed. It works with NDUFAF3, with which it is physically associated and whose deficiency produces a similar assembly defect. Without NDUFAF4 the Q-module intermediates it normally marks are not detectable at all.

evidence.snippet: Lentiviral complementation of patient fibroblasts with wild-type NDUFAF4 rescued complex I deficiency and the assembly defect, confirming the causal role of the variant.
evidence.explanation: The rescue that ties this node to the gene rather than to a coincidental variant.

genes/0.notes:
NDUFAF4 (HGNC:21034, "NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase complex assembly factor 4") is at 6q16.1. Its previous symbol is C6ORF66, which is the name under which the gene was discovered and the name used throughout the 2008 and 2013 literature; the HGNC record also lists the aliases HSPC125, bA22L21.1, My013 and HRPAP20, the last of which belongs to a separate line of breast-cancer work - the founding paper closes by noting that the same gene product had been shown to promote breast cancer cell invasiveness. None of that is part of this disease, and a literature search on the gene symbol will return a good deal of it.
Two facts about the allelic series bear on how a new variant should be read. The alleles span missense, frameshift and nonsense classes, and the truncating one is at the severe pole - but so is a missense allele, so allele class alone does not predict severity. And the optic-atrophy alleles sit in a well-modelled globular domain, distant from the N-terminal positions of the Leigh-associated alleles, which is the observation behind the open genotype-phenotype discussion.

evidence.snippet: Visual improvement was variable, with only 3 of 13 patients showing some degree of response to idebenone treatment
evidence.explanation: The observed response in the cohort that contains the NDUFAF4 patients. It is the reason this block is worded as a recommendation rather than as an effective treatment.

treatments/0.description:
A recommendation rather than a result, and it applies only to the optic-atrophy pole.
The 2026 series that found the NDUFAF4 optic-atrophy patients concludes that patients with nuclear complex I optic neuropathy may benefit from idebenone, dosed as for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, where it is an approved therapy. Its rationale is mechanistic: reduced idebenone can bypass complex I and hand electrons from NADH directly to complex III, so any complex I defect might be partially corrected by it.
What the same paper reports about its own cohort is discouraging, and should be read alongside the recommendation: visual improvement was variable, with only three of thirteen patients showing some degree of response. Those thirteen are not thirteen NDUFAF4 patients - the sentence sits in a paragraph describing the whole thirty-one-patient series, directly after the list of drugs used, so the thirteen are most plausibly the patients who received idebenone. No response rate can be attributed to this genotype from it, and no individual NDUFAF4 patient's treatment or outcome is reported. Nothing at all has been reported for the severe pole, where an optic-nerve-directed therapy would not address the encephalopathy.

treatments/1.description:
A preclinical attempt at a gene-directed therapy. Recombinant NDUFAF4 was fused to the HIV TAT cell-penetrating peptide, expressed in E. coli, purified, and applied to fibroblasts from a patient in the founding family. The fusion protein reached the cells and their mitochondria, raised complex I activity and ATP production, increased cell number, and lowered reactive oxygen species.
It has never left cell culture. There is no animal work, no pharmacokinetics, no dosing and no trial - and the delivery problem this approach would have to solve in a patient is exactly the one cell culture does not test, since the affected organs are brain and optic nerve. It is curated because it is a real, published, mechanism-directed intervention for this specific gene, and because the alternative - listing nothing under treatments - would misrepresent the state of the field.
No therapeutic_agent is bound: no CHEBI or NCIT term names a TAT-NDUFAF4 fusion protein, and binding a term for something else would be worse than leaving the slot empty.

open_questions/0.rationale:
The clinical range of this gene is as wide as any in the MC1DN series - fatal neonatal encephalopathy at one end, isolated optic atrophy at the other - and there is one structural observation that might explain it.
The 2026 series notes that the optic-atrophy missense allele p.I138T lies in a well-modelled globular domain of NDUFAF4, clearly distant from the Leigh-associated variants reported previously, which affect the N-terminus. It offers a reason why that might matter: N-terminal variants may impair mitochondrial import of the assembly factor rather than its function once inside, which would reduce the amount of protein reaching the matrix at all. A severe import defect and a partial functional defect would be expected to differ in severity.
Three things stop this being a finding. The prediction is in silico, from AlphaFold models and folding-stability predictors; no import assay has been done on any NDUFAF4 allele. The correlation is not clean even in the reported patients: the optic-atrophy proband from Family S carries the p.I138T globular-domain allele in trans with a frameshift, p.(P75Lfs*7), which should behave as a null and yet the phenotype is still isolated optic atrophy. And the founding family undercuts any simple genotype rule from a different direction: one patient with the same homozygous allele as five relatives who had infantile encephalomyopathy presented instead with antenatal cardiomyopathy, so within-genotype variation is already documented for this gene.
Why it matters: a laboratory reporting a new biallelic NDUFAF4 genotype has no basis for prognosis today. The experiment that would create one is a mitochondrial import and steady-state abundance assay across the reported allelic series, which is small enough to do exhaustively.

treatments/1.description: Catheterization or vesicostomy can improve bladder drainage when medication alone does not adequately empty the bladder.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports catheterization or vesicostomy as bladder-drainage management.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Bladder drainage reduces residual urine and infection risk.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends ocular lubrication for nocturnal lagophthalmos.

treatments/2.description: Lubricant eye drops during the day and eye ointment at night can protect the ocular surface in nocturnal lagophthalmos.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports prompt antibiotic treatment for acute urinary tract infections.

evidence.snippet: Approximately 4% of the US population aged 12 and older (10.1 million people) misused opioids in 2019
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how widespread the exposure modelled by this entry is, which is what makes a necessary-but-not-sufficient exposure epidemiologically significant.

evidence.snippet: Gene-based analyses identified novel genome-wide significant associations with PPP6C and FURIN.
evidence.explanation: Documents the loci beyond OPRM1 that this susceptibility node represents.

evidence.snippet: The current study identified OUD variant associations at OPRM1, single variant associations with FURIN, and 18 GWS associations in the OUD-MTAG.
evidence.explanation: The largest OUD-specific GWAS independently replicates the two loci this node carries, and finds nothing else at genome-wide significance for diagnosed OUD without multi-trait augmentation.

evidence.snippet: The genetic architecture of OUD is likely influenced by both OUD-specific loci and loci shared across SUDs.
evidence.explanation: Bounds every additional locus curated in the `genetic` section: signals recovered by multi-trait analysis are partly shared across substance use disorders rather than opioid-specific.

steps/3.description: Inherited liability is polygenic and, relative to other substance use disorders, unusually concentrated on the opioid receptor gene itself. OPRM1 carries the only long-replicated genome-wide significant signal; gene-based analysis has added FURIN and PPP6C. Genetic loading modifies the probability that opioid exposure escalates to compulsive use; it does not cause the disorder without exposure.

evidence.snippet: Opioids are powerful drugs that usurp and overpower the reward function of endogenous opioids and engage dramatic tolerance and withdrawal via molecular and neurocircuitry neuroadaptations within the same reward system.
evidence.explanation: Frames exogenous opioid action as hijacking the endogenous opioid reward system, the premise of this node.

steps/4.description: Prescription opioids, heroin, and illicit synthetic opioids such as fentanyl act as agonists at the mu-opioid receptor, a Gi/Go-coupled GPCR. Receptor activation inhibits adenylyl cyclase and opens GIRK potassium channels, hyperpolarizing the target neuron. The same receptor event underlies analgesia, euphoria, tolerance, and — in the brainstem — respiratory depression, which is why the therapeutic and lethal effects of opioids cannot be pharmacologically separated at this node.

evidence.snippet: A major problem in treating painful conditions is that tolerance limits the long-term utility of opioid agonists.
evidence.explanation: Establishes tolerance as the central clinical consequence of the receptor regulation this node models.

evidence.snippet: While some functional MOR regulatory mechanisms contributing to tolerance are clearly understood, there are large gaps in understanding the molecular processes responsible for loss of MOR function after chronic exposure to opioids.
evidence.explanation: The authors state explicitly that the molecular basis of chronic tolerance is incompletely understood, so this node's mechanism is only partially established.

steps/5.description: Chronic agonist exposure produces receptor phosphorylation, desensitization, and internalization, so that progressively higher doses are needed for the same effect. Tolerance to analgesia and euphoria is what drives dose escalation; critically, tolerance to respiratory depression develops incompletely and is lost quickly during abstinence, which is the pharmacological basis of the post-detoxification and post-release overdose spike.

evidence.snippet: Such negative emotional states that drive negative reinforcement are hypothesized to derive from the within-system dysregulation of key neurochemical circuits that mediate incentive-salience and/or reward systems (dopamine, opioid peptides) in the ventral striatum
evidence.explanation: Identifies ventral striatal dopamine and opioid peptide circuits as the reward system that later dysregulates. Support is partial because this review describes the dysregulation rather than the acute disinhibition step itself.

steps/6.description: Mu-opioid receptor agonism on ventral tegmental GABAergic interneurons removes their inhibitory tone on dopaminergic projection neurons, increasing dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens. This disinhibition route is the positive reinforcement of early use, and it is mechanistically distinct from the direct dopamine-releasing action of stimulants.

evidence.snippet: Morphine non-stereoselectively induced TLR4 signaling in vitro, blocked by a classical TLR4 antagonist and non-stereoselectively by naloxone.
evidence.explanation: Non-stereoselective activation blocked by a TLR4 antagonist is what establishes this as a TLR4 event rather than a mu-opioid receptor one.

evidence.snippet: TLR4 opposition to opioid actions was supported by morphine treatment of TLR4 knockout mice, which revealed a significant threefold leftward shift in the analgesia dose response function, versus wildtype mice.
evidence.explanation: Genetic removal of TLR4 shifts the morphine dose-response, giving a loss-of-function line of evidence independent of the pharmacology.

evidence.snippet: Although overall SOWS scores did not differ between groups, exploratory analyses pooling the two ibudilast groups demonstrated that they had lower ratings of withdrawal symptoms
evidence.explanation: The only human interventional test of this node available here. The prespecified comparison was null and the supportive result is an exploratory pooled subscale analysis, so it corroborates the node weakly and is recorded as PARTIAL rather than SUPPORT.

steps/7.description:
A non-classical, non-opioid-receptor arm of opioid action: opioids and some of their metabolites activate the TLR4/MD-2 innate immune complex on microglia and other myeloid cells, driving proinflammatory glial activation that opposes analgesia and contributes to analgesic tolerance, hyperalgesia, and withdrawal behaviour. The pharmacology is distinctive — activation is non-stereoselective, so it is not mediated by the mu-opioid receptor, and it is blocked by classical TLR4 antagonists. This node is deliberately kept parallel to, not upstream of, `Mu-Opioid Receptor Desensitization and Tolerance`: it is a second route to the same clinical endpoints rather than a cause of receptor-level desensitization.
The arm is well evidenced in rodents and in vitro and only weakly corroborated in people; see the `oud_tlr4_glial_human_translation` discussion for that mismatch, and the bounding evidence below for its dose-dependence.

evidence.snippet: Lofexidine is an FDA-approved, alpha2-adrenergic receptor agonist for treatment of OWS.
evidence.explanation: That an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist is an approved treatment for opioid withdrawal is pharmacological support for a noradrenergic substrate; the trial does not itself demonstrate the cAMP-PKA mechanism, so support is partial.

steps/8.description: Opioid agonism acutely inhibits adenylyl cyclase in locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons; chronic exposure drives a compensatory upregulation of the cAMP-PKA cascade. While drug is present the two oppose each other and firing is near normal. This is the classic opponent-process substrate of opioid physical dependence.

evidence.snippet: Fear of opioid withdrawal syndrome (OWS) often dissuades opioid discontinuation.
evidence.explanation: Documents the aversiveness of the syndrome and its role as a barrier to cessation, which is the behavioural significance this node carries.

evidence.snippet: However, they also engage the brain systems for stress and pain (somatic and emotional) while producing hyperalgesia and hyperkatifeia, which drive pronounced drug-seeking behavior via processes of negative reinforcement.
evidence.explanation: Links the stress and pain systems engaged in withdrawal to negative-reinforcement drug seeking.

steps/9.description: On cessation or antagonist administration, unopposed noradrenergic hyperactivity produces the characteristic syndrome: rhinorrhea, lacrimation, mydriasis, piloerection, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, insomnia, and dysphoria. It is intensely aversive but, unlike alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, rarely life-threatening in itself — its clinical danger is that it drives return to use, and that abstinence resets tolerance.

evidence.snippet: Compelling evidence indicates that plasticity in the brain pain emotional systems is triggered by acute excessive drug intake and becomes sensitized during the development of compulsive drug taking with repeated withdrawal.
evidence.explanation: Supports drug-induced plasticity in emotion-related systems during the development of compulsive use. This review does not itself demonstrate the prefrontal executive deficit, so support is partial and a prefrontal-specific citation is a curation gap.

steps/10.description: Impaired top-down inhibitory control over drug seeking, with altered prefrontal-limbic connectivity. This is the preoccupation/anticipation arm of the addiction cycle, and it removes the counterweight to both cue-driven and withdrawal-driven use.

evidence.snippet: Such negative emotional states that drive negative reinforcement are hypothesized to derive from the within-system dysregulation of key neurochemical circuits that mediate incentive-salience and/or reward systems (dopamine, opioid peptides) in the ventral striatum and from the between-system recruitment of brain stress systems (corticotropin-releasing factor, dynorphin, norepinephrine, hypocretin, vasopressin, glucocorticoids, and neuroimmune factors) in the extended amygdala.
evidence.explanation: Names both arms — within-system reward deficit and between-system stress recruitment — and their anatomy.

evidence.snippet: In animal models, repeated extended access to drugs or opioids results in negative emotion-like states, reflected by the elevation of reward thresholds, lower pain thresholds, anxiety-like behavior, and dysphoric-like responses.
evidence.explanation: Provides the preclinical operationalization of the negative emotional state, including the elevated reward threshold that defines reward deficit.

steps/11.description: The withdrawal/negative-affect stage combines a within-system reward deficit (reduced dopaminergic and opioid-peptide tone in ventral striatum) with between-system recruitment of extended-amygdala stress mediators — corticotropin-releasing factor, dynorphin, norepinephrine, hypocretin, glucocorticoids. The resulting dysphoria, anxiety, and anhedonia extend into protracted abstinence and drive relapse by negative reinforcement.

evidence.snippet: Opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH) is defined as a state of nociceptive sensitization caused by exposure to opioids.
evidence.explanation: Defines the phenomenon this node models.

evidence.snippet: It is generally thought to result from neuroplastic changes in the peripheral and central nervous system (CNS) that lead to sensitization of pronociceptive pathways.
evidence.explanation: States the sensitization mechanism that distinguishes hyperalgesia from receptor-level tolerance.

evidence.snippet: Findings of the clinical prevalence of OIH are not available.
evidence.explanation: The review states that clinical prevalence is unknown, so no frequency claim can be attached to this node.

steps/12.description: Paradoxical nociceptive sensitization caused by opioid exposure, in which a patient receiving opioids becomes more sensitive to painful stimuli. It is mechanistically distinct from tolerance — sensitization of pronociceptive pathways rather than loss of receptor responsiveness — and it matters clinically because it can be mistaken for undertreated pain and answered with a dose increase that worsens it.

evidence.snippet: However, they also engage the brain systems for stress and pain (somatic and emotional) while producing hyperalgesia and hyperkatifeia, which drive pronounced drug-seeking behavior via processes of negative reinforcement.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the negative-reinforcement drive toward the compulsive drug-seeking endpoint this node represents.

steps/13.description: The convergent clinical endpoint: compulsive opioid seeking and use despite harm, with impaired control over intake. Three motivational routes feed it — positive reinforcement early, negative reinforcement from withdrawal and hyperkatifeia later, and escalating pain from hyperalgesia — while prefrontal executive deficit removes the brake.

evidence.snippet: Opioid-induced respiratory depression (OIRD), the primary cause of opioid-induced death, is the neural depression of respiratory drive which, together with a decreased level of consciousness and obstructive sleep apnea, cause ventilatory insufficiency.
evidence.explanation: Establishes respiratory depression as the mechanism of opioid death and names its three components.

evidence.snippet: Deletion of μ opioid receptors from neurons showed that the preBötC and KF/PBN contribute to OIRD with the KF as a respiratory modulator and the preBötC as inspiratory rhythm generator.
evidence.explanation: Receptor-deletion experiments localize the effect to specific brainstem nuclei, giving the anatomical claim causal support.

steps/14.description: Mu-opioid receptors on brainstem respiratory neurons — the preBotzinger complex, which generates inspiratory rhythm, and the Kolliker-Fuse and parabrachial nuclei, which modulate breathing — mediate depression of respiratory drive. Combined with reduced consciousness and airway obstruction this produces ventilatory insufficiency. This is the proximate cause of opioid-induced death and the target of naloxone.

evidence.snippet: Variability of responses to opioids and individual differences in physiological and neurological states (e.g., anesthesia, sleep-disordered breathing, concurrent drug administration) add to the risk.
evidence.explanation: Supports the claim that overdose risk is modified by physiological state and concurrent drugs rather than being a fixed property of the dose.

steps/15.description: Death from ventilatory insufficiency. Risk is not a simple function of disorder severity: it is dominated by tolerance state (sharply elevated after detoxification or incarceration), by co-ingested sedatives, and by the potency of the illicit supply. This is why overdose risk can rise at precisely the moment a person stops using.

evidence.snippet: However, they also engage the brain systems for stress and pain (somatic and emotional) while producing hyperalgesia and hyperkatifeia, which drive pronounced drug-seeking behavior via processes of negative reinforcement.
evidence.explanation: Compulsive drug seeking is the defining feature of the disorder, so it is present in essentially all cases; that is the basis for VERY_FREQUENT.

steps/16.description: Compulsive opioid use with impaired control — using more or longer than intended, unsuccessful efforts to cut down, and continued use despite knowledge of harm. The defining clinical feature.

evidence.snippet: Self-reported opioid craving was initially less with XR-NTX than with BUP-NX (p=0·0012), then converged by week 24 (p=0·20).
evidence.explanation: Craving is measured as a distinct prospective endpoint in OUD pharmacotherapy trials, separable from consumption measures.

steps/17.description: A strong desire or urge to use opioids — a DSM-5 criterion and a common trial endpoint.

evidence.snippet: Opioid-induced respiratory depression (OIRD), the primary cause of opioid-induced death, is the neural depression of respiratory drive which, together with a decreased level of consciousness and obstructive sleep apnea, cause ventilatory insufficiency.
evidence.explanation: Supports the intoxication syndrome including depressed consciousness; the review does not itself document miosis, so a miosis-specific citation is a curation gap.

steps/18.description: Pinpoint pupils, a cardinal sign of acute opioid intoxication and part of the classic overdose triad with respiratory depression and depressed consciousness.

evidence.snippet: Opioid-induced respiratory depression (OIRD), the primary cause of opioid-induced death, is the neural depression of respiratory drive which, together with a decreased level of consciousness and obstructive sleep apnea, cause ventilatory insufficiency.
evidence.explanation: Directly documents respiratory depression and its lethal significance.

steps/19.description: Depression of respiratory drive from brainstem mu-opioid receptor activation; the proximate cause of opioid-related death and the target of naloxone reversal.

evidence.snippet: Variability of responses to opioids and individual differences in physiological and neurological states (e.g., anesthesia, sleep-disordered breathing, concurrent drug administration) add to the risk.
evidence.explanation: Identifies sleep-disordered breathing as a state that compounds opioid-induced respiratory risk.

steps/20.description: Central and obstructive apnoea associated with chronic opioid use, contributing to ventilatory insufficiency during overdose.

evidence.snippet: efficacy was assessed using the Short Opioid Withdrawal Scale of Gossop (SOWS-G) daily
evidence.explanation: Withdrawal severity is scored on standardized scales that include objective autonomic signs; the abstract does not enumerate individual signs, so support for mydriasis specifically is partial.

steps/21.description: Pupillary dilation during opioid withdrawal — the direction opposite to the miosis of intoxication, and one of the objective signs scored on withdrawal rating scales.

evidence.snippet: Fear of opioid withdrawal syndrome (OWS) often dissuades opioid discontinuation.
evidence.explanation: Supports the existence and clinical salience of the withdrawal syndrome; the abstract does not enumerate its individual signs, so support for rhinorrhea specifically is partial.

steps/22.description: Rhinorrhea and lacrimation during opioid withdrawal.

evidence.snippet: Fear of opioid withdrawal syndrome (OWS) often dissuades opioid discontinuation.
evidence.explanation: Supports the withdrawal syndrome as a whole; a sign-level citation is a curation gap.

steps/23.description: Diarrhoea and abdominal cramping during opioid withdrawal.

evidence.snippet: Fear of opioid withdrawal syndrome (OWS) often dissuades opioid discontinuation.
evidence.explanation: Supports the withdrawal syndrome as a whole; a sign-level citation is a curation gap.

steps/24.description: Nausea and vomiting during opioid withdrawal.

evidence.snippet: However, they also engage the brain systems for stress and pain (somatic and emotional) while producing hyperalgesia and hyperkatifeia, which drive pronounced drug-seeking behavior via processes of negative reinforcement.
evidence.explanation: Supports somatic pain as part of the withdrawal state; not a myalgia-specific measurement.

steps/25.description: Diffuse muscle and joint pain during opioid withdrawal.

evidence.snippet: Hypotension and bradycardia were more common with lofexidine.
