steps/23.description: Congenital cardiovascular anomalies include patent ductus arteriosus, atrial or ventricular septal defects, and tetralogy of Fallot.

evidence.snippet: In our case the patient exhibited a chronic rash of livedo reticularis with telangiectasia on her legs. Abnormally pigmented lesions and cutis mamorata were reported in the original WABS case.
evidence.explanation: Documents the spectrum and recurrence of cutaneous pigmentation findings.

steps/24.description: Reported pigmentary and vascular-pattern findings include café-au-lait macules, hypo- or hyperpigmentation, cutis marmorata, and livedo reticularis with telangiectasia.

evidence.snippet: Abnormal skin pigmentation and genitourinary malformations have also been reported.
evidence.explanation: Supports genitourinary malformations as part of the reported spectrum.

steps/25.description: Hypoplastic scrotum, cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and multicystic kidneys have been reported in individual cases.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, a DNA binding DDX11 mutant failed to correct SCC in WABS cells and DDX11 deficiency reduced replication fork speed.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates both fork slowing and failed cohesion rescue after DDX11 dysfunction.

edges/1.description: Loss of DDX11 DNA binding and fork-localized function slows forks and compromises recruitment or stabilization of cohesin during replication.

evidence.snippet: Defective DDX11 is associated with a unique cellular phenotype in which features of Fanconi anemia (drug-induced chromosomal breakage) and Roberts syndrome (sister chromatid cohesion defects) coexist.
evidence.explanation: Establishes induced breakage in the founding patient-cell model.

edges/2.description: DDX11-deficient cells can become hypersensitive to DNA cross-linking stress, although this phenotype is not penetrant across all affected individuals.

evidence.snippet: DDX11 is a novel nucleolar protein that preferentially binds to hypomethylated active ribosomal DNA (rDNA) gene loci, where it interacts with upstream binding factor (UBF) and the RNA polymerase I (Pol I).
evidence.explanation: Defines the direct nucleolar and rDNA role perturbed by DDX11 loss.

edges/3.description: Loss of nucleolar DDX11 binding shifts active rDNA toward heterochromatin and reduces recruitment of the RNA polymerase I machinery.

evidence.snippet: The DDX11-Timeless interaction is critical for sister chromatid cohesion in interphase and mitosis.
evidence.explanation: Directly links the fork-protection interaction to cohesion.

edges/4.description: Failure to couple cohesin to DNA replication reduces functional cohesion.

evidence.snippet: separation of the sister chromatids and centromeres during metaphase rather than in anaphase visible on C-banding techniques
evidence.explanation: Defines the cytogenetic consequence of the cohesion defect.

edges/5.description: Insufficient cohesion permits premature separation of chromatids and centromeres, producing the characteristic railroad-track appearance.

evidence.snippet: The mutant embryos were smaller in size, malformed and exhibited sparse cellularity in comparison to normal or heterozygous litter mates.
evidence.explanation: Supports an in-vivo developmental consequence of complete Ddx11 loss, but not the organ-specific pathway in surviving humans.

edges/6.description: A developmental consequence is plausible from animal loss-of-function models, but the relevant human tissues and intervening mechanisms are unknown.

evidence.snippet: DDX11 knockdown changed the epigenetic state of rDNA loci from euchromatic structures to more heterochromatic structures, reduced the activity of UBF, decreased the recruitment of UBF and RPA194 (a subunit of Pol I) to rDNA promoter, suppressed rRNA transcription and thereby inhibited growth and proliferation of HeLa cells.
evidence.explanation: Directly links the rDNA transcription defect to impaired proliferation.

edges/7.description: Suppressed rRNA transcription reduces growth and proliferation in the cell model.

evidence.snippet: Knockdown of the zebrafish ortholog of human DDX11 by morpholinos resulted in growth retardation and vertebral and craniofacial malformations in zebrafish, concomitant with the changes in histone epigenetic modifications at rDNA loci, the reduction of Pol I recruitment to the rDNA promoter and a significant decrease in nascent pre-RNA levels.
evidence.explanation: Couples rDNA readouts to developmental abnormalities in vivo, while remaining indirect for human disease.

edges/8.description: Reduced cell production is proposed to impair embryonic growth and organogenesis, with tissue-specific intermediates unresolved.

edges/9.description: Prenatal growth failure is universal in reported individuals, but the causal tissue and cellular bottleneck are not established.

edges/10.description: Persistent growth deficiency may reflect reduced cell production and nutritional factors; their relative contributions are unknown.

edges/11.description: Reduced prenatal brain growth is plausibly downstream of impaired development, but neural progenitor-specific causality has not been tested.

edges/12.description: Structural brain anomalies occur in a minority of affected individuals, but their lineage-specific developmental mechanism remains unknown.

edges/13.description: Poor sulcation, delayed gyration, and focal lissencephaly implicate cortical development through untested neural-progenitor intermediates.

edges/14.description: Callosal hypoplasia is plausibly developmental, but no DDX11-dependent axon-guidance or commissural-neuron mechanism has been demonstrated.

edges/15.description: Vermian hypoplasia is reported clinically, but the affected progenitor population and causal molecular branch are unresolved.

edges/16.description: Hearing impairment reflects abnormal cochlear development; the relevant embryonic cell population and molecular route from DDX11 remain unknown.

edges/17.description: The tissue-selective basis of cochlear hypoplasia is unresolved.

edges/18.description: Cognitive impairment is associated with congenital brain growth and hearing-language effects, but its direct cellular mechanism is unknown.

edges/19.description: Severe hearing impairment is a known contributor to speech delay, while intellectual disability may additionally limit receptive language.

edges/20.description: Mild developmental delay is variably present; affected developmental programs have not been defined.

edges/21.description: Craniofacial patterning is affected, but the cellular route is unknown.

edges/22.description: Limb and skeletal development can be affected through unknown intermediates.

edges/23.description: Congenital cardiac anomalies are variably present; their mechanism is unknown.

edges/24.description: Pigmentary abnormalities are variably present; the responsible cell lineage is unknown.

edges/25.description: Genitourinary malformations occur in some individuals through unknown developmental intermediates.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report a human individual with biallelic mutations in DDX11.
evidence.explanation: The founding report identifies biallelic DDX11 variants in WABS.

evidence.snippet: Biochemical studies of purified recombinant DDX11 indicated that the p.R263Q mutation impaired DDX11 helicase activity by perturbing its DNA binding and DNA-dependent ATP hydrolysis.
evidence.explanation: Provides functional evidence for a disease-associated allele.

evidence.snippet: DDX11 | HGNC:2736 | Warsaw breakage syndrome | MONDO:0013252 | AR | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the autosomal recessive DDX11-WABS gene-disease relationship as definitive.

evidence.snippet: Supplementary formula and/or gastrostomy tube as needed to optimize nutrition.
evidence.explanation: Provides the GeneReviews nutrition recommendation.

treatments/0.description: Optimize nutrition for poor weight gain; supplementary formula and gastrostomy feeding can be used when needed. This is supportive care and does not correct the underlying DDX11 defect.

evidence.snippet: Treatments for hearing loss include hearing aids; cochlear implantation; auditory brain stem implant for individuals with profound hearing loss due to missing or nonfunctioning cochlea or auditory nerve; establishing a system of communication and hearing habilitation that may include sign language, auditory therapy, and speech therapy; and educational programs designed for individuals with hearing impairment.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the anatomy-dependent hearing and communication options.

treatments/1.description: Management depends on residual cochlear and cochlear-nerve anatomy and can include hearing aids, cochlear implantation when a cochlear nerve is present, or an auditory brainstem implant for profound loss with absent or nonfunctioning cochlea or auditory nerve. Communication support should begin promptly and may include sign language, auditory therapy, speech-language therapy, and hearing-focused education.

evidence.snippet: Early intervention and educational support; physical, occupational, and speech therapies
evidence.explanation: States the recommended developmental supports.

treatments/2.description: Provide early intervention and individualized educational support, with physical, occupational, and speech-language therapy according to need.

evidence.snippet: treatment of cardiac anomalies per cardiologist; treatment of limb anomalies per orthopedist with occupational therapy as needed; treatment of genitourinary anomalies per nephrologist and/or urologist.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports specialist-directed supportive management.

treatments/3.description: Treat congenital cardiac anomalies with cardiology, limb anomalies with orthopedics and occupational therapy, and genitourinary anomalies with nephrology or urology. Management is individualized and supportive.

evidence.snippet: Monitor growth, speech development, and educational needs with each visit; behavioral assessment for ADHD as needed; there is no consensus regarding tumor screening.
evidence.explanation: States the longitudinal surveillance recommendations and tumor-screening uncertainty.

treatments/4.description: Measure height, weight, head circumference, and body mass index and review speech development and educational needs at every visit. Assess for ADHD or other behavioral concerns when clinically indicated. There is no consensus for tumor screening because malignancy risk remains unproven.

evidence.snippet: Once the DDX11 pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: Supports cascade and reproductive testing after familial variant identification.

treatments/5.description: Counsel families about autosomal recessive inheritance and the 25% recurrence risk when both parents carry a pathogenic variant. Once familial DDX11 variants are known, offer carrier testing to at-risk relatives and discuss prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing.

evidence.snippet: Collectively, our results establish a critical role for the DDX11-Timeless interaction in coordinating DNA replication with sister chromatid cohesion, and have important implications for understanding the molecular basis of WABS.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports replication-coupled cohesion as the canonical model.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, a DNA binding DDX11 mutant failed to correct SCC in WABS cells and DDX11 deficiency reduced replication fork speed.
evidence.explanation: Connects disease-cell cohesion rescue to replication-fork slowing.

hypotheses/0.description: The best-supported model places DDX11 at nascent DNA with the fork-protection factor Timeless, where it promotes cohesin association during DNA replication. Pathogenic DDX11 dysfunction slows replication forks and impairs sister chromatid cohesion, producing premature chromatid separation and a variable genotoxin-sensitive chromosome-instability phenotype. How these cellular defects produce organ-selective congenital abnormalities is not yet known.

evidence.snippet: DDX11 knockdown changed the epigenetic state of rDNA loci from euchromatic structures to more heterochromatic structures, reduced the activity of UBF, decreased the recruitment of UBF and RPA194 (a subunit of Pol I) to rDNA promoter, suppressed rRNA transcription and thereby inhibited growth and proliferation of HeLa cells.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the rDNA-transcription and proliferation branch in cells.

evidence.snippet: These growth disruptions in zebrafish in response to DDX11 reduction showed similarities to the clinically described developmental abnormalities found in WABS patients for the first time in any vertebrate.
evidence.explanation: Provides in-vivo developmental support, but only in a morpholino model and without proving the same pathway causes human manifestations.

hypotheses/1.description: DDX11 also binds active rDNA, interacts with UBF and RNA polymerase I, and supports rRNA transcription. DDX11 depletion shifts rDNA toward heterochromatin, suppresses rRNA synthesis, and reduces proliferation; a zebrafish knockdown model couples the same molecular readouts to growth and craniofacial abnormalities. This may act alongside the canonical cohesion mechanism, but a causal contribution to human organ-specific disease has not been demonstrated.

evidence.snippet: These growth disruptions in zebrafish in response to DDX11 reduction showed similarities to the clinically described developmental abnormalities found in WABS patients for the first time in any vertebrate.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates partial model convergence but not the human organ-specific causal bridge, which is why the item remains open.

open_questions/0.rationale: The fork/cohesion and rDNA branches are experimentally reproducible, but no disease-relevant human neural, cochlear, cardiac, or embryonic model connects either branch to the defining congenital phenotype. Resolving this bridge is necessary before any organ-specific mechanism or disease-modifying target can be considered established.

evidence.snippet: The absence of Ddx11 resulted in embryonic lethality at E10.5.
evidence.explanation: Defines the central severity mismatch of the available mouse model.

open_questions/1.rationale: The null mouse demonstrates gene necessity but dies before relevant organ phenotypes can be assessed, while the zebrafish model is transient and only partially phenocopies WABS. Patient-variant knock-in models, ideally with lineage-resolved neural and inner-ear readouts, are needed.

evidence.snippet: Surveillance: Monitor growth, speech development, and educational needs with each visit; behavioral assessment for ADHD as needed; there is no consensus regarding tumor screening.
evidence.explanation: Documents the current surveillance scope and tumor-screening uncertainty.

open_questions/2.rationale: Published cohorts are small, most affected individuals are children, and no consensus tumor-screening protocol exists. A longitudinal registry is needed to distinguish true late complications from isolated observations and to assess whether DNA-damaging therapies require special precautions.

evidence.snippet: RNA-seq revealed marked upregulation of SERF1B, which was validated in fetal tissue. Mechanistically, SERF1B overexpression may accelerate SNCA protein aggregation and exacerbate neurotoxicity.
evidence.explanation: States the newly proposed molecular pathway and its limited validation.

open_questions/3.rationale: A 2026 study reported this pathway using variants from one family, a transfected neural-cell model, RNA sequencing, and validation in fetal tissue. Independent patient-derived neural models, protein-aggregation measurements, genetic rescue, and replication across alleles are needed before it can enter the core disease graph.

evidence.snippet: The disease is a chronic infection of the intestinal mucosa with the bacterium Tropheryma whipplei, which leads to a lymphostasis with an impaired absorption of the nutrition.
evidence.explanation: Review describes lymphatic obstruction and malabsorption from chronic infection.

evidence.snippet: Recent studies suggest that a host-specific dysfunction of the intestinal macrophages is responsible for the chronic infection with T. whipplei.
evidence.explanation: Highlights macrophage functional defect underlying persistent infection.

steps/0.description: Chronic small bowel infection by Tropheryma whipplei leads to lymphostasis and impaired nutrient absorption driven by macrophage dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: Etanercept, adalimumab or certolizumab treatment of monocyte-derived macrophages from healthy subjects significantly increased bacterial replication in vitro without affecting uptake.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates TNF inhibitors increase T. whipplei replication within macrophages.

evidence.snippet: TNFI aggravate/exacerbate latent or subclinical undiagnosed Whipple's disease by promoting a strong inflammatory response and apoptosis.
evidence.explanation: Study links TNF blockade to apoptosis-driven exacerbation of Whipple disease.

steps/1.description: Anti-TNF biologics can reprogram macrophages infected with Tropheryma whipplei, increasing bacterial replication and macrophage apoptosis, exacerbating latent disease.

evidence.snippet: The ribosome is one of the main antibiotic targets in the bacterial cell.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the bacterial ribosome as the doxycycline (tetracycline) target, the step this node represents. Evidence source is OTHER as this is a review.

steps/2.description: Tropheryma whipplei depends on 70S-ribosome translation. Doxycycline binds the 30S subunit and arrests bacterial protein synthesis; it anchors the alternative long-course oral regimen (with hydroxychloroquine) and lifelong relapse prophylaxis.

evidence.snippet: The other two enzyme families are involved in the synthesis of tetrahydrofolate (THF), i.e. dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS) and dihydrofolate reductase.
evidence.explanation: Establishes DHPS and DHFR (the sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim targets) in folate synthesis, the step this node represents. Evidence source is OTHER as this is a review article.

steps/3.description: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) — the standard oral maintenance therapy after ceftriaxone induction — inhibits the T. whipplei folate pathway at two enzymes: sulfamethoxazole blocks dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS) and trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), giving synergistic sequential blockade.

evidence.snippet: Half the world's population is exposed to T. whipplei, but only one in a million develop WD. This suggests that acquired or inborn errors of immunity (IEI) may underlie WD.
evidence.explanation: Genetic review links rare immune defects to disease susceptibility.

evidence.snippet: Anti-TNF treatment is a well established risk factor for flare-ups of WD.
evidence.explanation: Notes iatrogenic immune suppression as a trigger for disease activation.

evidence.snippet: About 60% were immunosuppressed. The most frequent clinical presentations were joint pain (16/22), weight loss (15/22) and/or digestive tract disorder (15/22).
evidence.explanation: Cohort shows high immunosuppression rate among confirmed Whipple disease cases.

evidence.snippet: The patient was admitted to the hospital due to recurrent diarrhea for 1 mo, shortness of breath, and 1 wk of fever, after 3 years of renal transplantation.
evidence.explanation: Post-transplant case illustrates Whipple disease emerging under chronic immunosuppression.

steps/4.description: Only a small fraction of exposed individuals develop Whipple disease, implicating rare inborn or acquired immune defects and risk from anti-TNF therapy.

evidence.snippet: although glycan chain polymerization occurs in the absence of transpeptidation (for example, in the presence of penicillin), efficient transpeptidation requires ongoing GTase reactions
evidence.explanation: Establishes that beta-lactams act by blocking PBP transpeptidation, the cross-linking step this node represents. Evidence source is OTHER as this is a review article.

steps/5.description: Tropheryma whipplei, an actinobacterium, builds and maintains its peptidoglycan cell wall by penicillin-binding protein (PBP) transpeptidase cross-linking. This essential, bacteria-specific reaction is the target of the intravenous ceftriaxone induction used in Whipple disease; beta-lactam acylation of the PBP active site halts cross-linking and provides the bactericidal induction phase before TMP-SMX maintenance.

evidence.snippet: The German treatment recommendations include a two-week intravenous induction therapy with ceftriaxone, which is followed by a three-month oral maintenance therapy with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.
evidence.explanation: Details standard ceftriaxone induction and TMP-SMX maintenance regimen.

treatments/0.description: Two-week intravenous ceftriaxone induction followed by oral TMP-SMX maintenance to eradicate infection and prevent relapse.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: The ceftriaxone induction component acylates the T. whipplei PBP transpeptidase, blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking.

treatments/0/targets/1.description: The TMP-SMX maintenance component blocks DHPS and DHFR in the folate pathway.

evidence.snippet: A French group favors a combination of doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine for 1 year, followed by a lifelong administration of doxycycline.
evidence.explanation: Review reports alternative long-course doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine approach.

treatments/1.description: Oral doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine for one year, followed by lifelong doxycycline for relapse prevention.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Doxycycline binds the 30S ribosome and arrests T. whipplei protein synthesis.
